title: Indigenous Just Transition in The Arctic
content:
This is going to be a collaborative event between Ungeirr Umkveraasenaar, or the Icelandic Young Environmentalists, and the Indigenous Environmental Network. Maybe we can go around and you guys can give a little introduction about yourselves. Sure.

Huang’a a’ka, pang’a’anang naka pang’a’u yu, huang’a a’taka, a’anatirma, naka kirstinuga pás, huang’a sivunga rumi. I come from St. Lawrence Island. I’ve been with IEN since 2021, and I work on organizing against climate geoengineering.

Kweyanaipaplusi maunga, huang’a a’akaluk, ungelaksirmiu runga, angayukang maktaklu Charlie. I a’anukwa’apu’a makigaklu anaktiyuk asii, janililu Charlie, chinirmiu, ungelaksirmiu. Thank you everyone for welcoming us here today.

I’m Adrienne A’akaluk Blatchford. I’m from Unalakleet, Alaska, which is up on the Northwest Coast in the passageway to the Arctic. We’re right on the coast of the Bering Sea in the heart of the Norton Sound.

And I work with Indigenous Environmental Network as a geoengineering outreach organizer with a focus on Alaska and the Arctic. Hello, thank you for having us as the host.

My name is Thomas Joseph. I’m a Hoopa Valley tribal member from the Six Rivers National Forest in Northern California. I am also Shoshone Paiute from the Sierra Nevadas. Paiute is what we call it, the land of flowing water.

title: KIITG Report September 2026
content:
Brenna Yellowthunder (Lead Coordinator, KIITG) spoke at the Oregon Data Center Moratorium Rally on Sept. 8 in Oregon’s capitol, Salem. Alongside Governor Kotek, they emphasized the effect hyper scale data centers have on rivers and salmon, a cornerstone of local tribes culture. They also joined the lobby day, urging state legislators to support a 3-year moratorium on data centers. The event was organized by the Columbia Riverkeepers, Food and Water Watch, and more.

Following the largest pipeline spill in Wisconsin last month, by Canadian pipeline giant Embridge, the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe declared a disaster for their reservation after the spill, and Chairperson Liz Arbuckle said, “This is what we said would happen.”

The break triggered a massive spill of 1.3 million gallons of natural gas liquids. Federal data shows the leak is the largest reported oil and gas spill ever in Wisconsin.

Michigan’s 12 federally recognized tribes led the Mackinac Bridge Walk, with several tribal chairs, chiefs, and presidents joining together to activate the ancestral Three Fires Confederacy’s first collective call to action.

On Labor Day, Sept. 7, 2026, roughly 34,000 people participated in the Mackinac Bridge Walk, with Michigan tribes leading a unified stand against Line 5.

title: No DAPL 10th Year Anniversary Reunion
content:
It is impossible to briefly summarize the NoDAPL fight and what it meant to us all. For the months we stood in Radical indigenous space, yes in ceremony and prayer, but also Direct Action. There were many conflicts external and internal so many of left feeling more broken than victorious.

Attendees pitched tents, a tipi, an outdoor kitchen, and a first-aid station. They erected a stage so people could stand before their friends and relatives and share their stories. Many faces familiar to those who took part in the uprising spoke about how Standing Rock changed their lives.

Healing and mourning was a central theme at the reunion. Tasina Sapa Win of Cheyenne River told those gathered that “these past 10 years, I fell into a really dark place, something I’m not really proud of, but it’s a part of my story and it’s a part of the story of a lot of folks who left camp.”

For so many of there are mixed feelings, joy at reuniting with people we stood beside during a brutal North Dakota winter, but also the difficulty of remembering the violence we collectively experienced on the frontlines.
